title: Called, Loved, and Kept
subtitle: Jude 1:1–2
description: A servant's signature and a kept people: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, greets those called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ, with mercy multiplied.
paragraphs: The shortest signature in this group of letters carries the least title a man could choose: “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ:” Servant comes first, before the family connection, as if Jude wanted his standing settled before his name meant anything. And the readers are described before they are greeted, in three words that all happen to them rather than from them: called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ. Kept is the letter's first quiet promise, and it will prove to be its last loud one too: the book that opens with readers kept in Christ closes with the God who is able to keep them from stumbling. Between those two keepings stands everything Jude is about to say about danger.

The greeting that follows is shaped like the letter itself: “Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.” Multiplied, not merely given; this writer reaches for increase where other greetings reach for grace. And mercy leads the list, which matters in a letter that will end by assigning mercy as work: mercy awaited at the close of the age, mercy shown to doubters, mercy tempered with fear at the fire's edge. The readers of the sternest page in this group are first covered in the thing the page will ask them to practice. Jude does not write like a man who enjoys severity. He writes like a man whose greetings run to mercy multiplied, which is worth remembering when the severity arrives.

Two plain statements belong here, once. Jude names himself a servant and James's brother and nothing more; tradition has long identified him with Jude the apostle, the one distinguished from Judas Iscariot, and his brother James with James the Lord's brother, whose own letter stands earlier in this series, and that identification is named as tradition, with no case argued for or against it in the telling. This book stands last in the undated group of this series, with no date given and none invented. What the letter itself insists on is narrower and warmer: a servant writes, to people who are called and loved and kept, and he wishes them more mercy than they already have.

What he does not do is begin with the letter he wanted to write. He had made every effort, he is about to say, to write about the salvation we share, and the effort was genuine; but something had crept into the churches while the kind letter was being prepared, and the servant's greeting gives way, one verse from here, to a compelled change of subject: a call to contend earnestly for a faith that was entrusted once for all.

title: Contend for the Faith
subtitle: Jude 1:3–4
description: The letter he meant to write set aside under compulsion: contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all, because certain men have crept in unnoticed and turned grace into license.
paragraphs: Every reader of this letter is reading a substitute. Jude says so in his third sentence, and the telling carries his explanation at face value: “Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints.” Made every effort: the kind letter was not a passing thought but a project under way, about the salvation we share, the common ground of writer and readers. Necessity overruled it. The Greek weight of his word is compulsion; circumstances reached into his desk and changed his subject, and a servant who had planned to write about shared joy found himself writing a call to arms instead.

The call itself has a particular shape, and it is worth hearing exactly: “contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints.” Contend is an athlete's word, struggle language, but the thing struggled for is a deposit, not a discovery: the faith entrusted, handed over, once for all, to the saints. Jude does not ask his readers to improve the faith, extend it, or defend their own additions to it. It was delivered complete, in a single delivery, and the contending is for its keeping. That is why this letter pairs so naturally with the keeper theme of its greeting; the people who are kept are now told to contend for what was entrusted to their keeping.

The necessity has a cause, and the verse breaks around it so the telling carries it as written: “For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed” and then, after the break, “ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.” Crept in is a side-door word, entry without announcement, and unnoticed is the congregation's part of the tragedy: they were inside before they were seen. Jude's three charges are precise. Their future was designated long ago, written down in the old words he is about to quote. Their doctrine turns grace, God's kindness to sinners, into a license for immorality, freedom redefined as permission. And their confession denies, in practice and teaching, our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ, the one title doubled against them.

No names are given, in Jude's letter or in this telling, and that is deliberate on both sides. He does not identify the men beyond their doctrine and their fruit, and no person, teacher, church, or movement of any later age is identified with them here; the description stands as his account of his own crisis, for his own readers, in his own words. What he does instead of naming them is older and, for his purpose, stronger: he reminds the church of its own archive, three judgments from the deep past that everyone in the room already knows. You are fully aware of this, he is about to say. I want to remind you anyway.

title: Remember the Judgments
subtitle: Jude 1:5–7
description: Three reminders from the archive: the people Jesus delivered out of Egypt and the unbelieving destroyed, the angels kept in chains under darkness, and Sodom and Gomorrah on display as an example.
paragraphs: The reminders begin with the most famous rescue in Israel's memory, and Jude states his method before he starts: “Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe.” Fully aware, and reminded anyway; that is the letter's pastoral logic in one sentence, that knowledge possessed is not the same as knowledge held in view. And the wording is carried here exactly as the Berean Bible gives it: Jesus is the named deliverer out of Egypt, and the same hand that delivered destroyed the unbelieving among the delivered. The telling does not smooth the sentence into the Exodus account's own wording; Jude's point depends on the pairing, salvation and judgment from the same Savior, inside the same rescued people. The warning is aimed at insiders, and Egypt is chosen because everyone in it had been saved first.

The second reminder leaves the human story altogether: “And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling” and then, after the sentence's own break, “these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day.” Jude gives no narrative for the angels, no names, no scene; their own books do not tell this fall either, and the telling adds none of it. What he gives is a boundary crossed, a dwelling abandoned, and a keeping that is the dark mirror of the readers' own: the God who keeps his people in Christ keeps these angels in chains, both keepings aimed at a day, theirs the judgment of the great day still ahead. Rank was no exemption. That is the reminder's edge for teachers who slander glorious beings: beings far more glorious than teachers have been chained for leaving their place.

The third reminder returns to earth and to display: “In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire.” On display is Jude's word for it: the cities stand in the record like an exhibit, not merely punished once but held up permanently, sustaining, in his striking phrase, the punishment of eternal fire as a standing lesson. Genesis told their story in its own place and this letter retells none of it; Jude takes from it exactly what his argument needs, the in-like-manner bridge to the dreamers of his own day, whose immorality he has already named as grace turned into license.

Three reminders, three realms: a nation, the angels, the cities. A people delivered and judged, spirits exalted and chained, cities flourishing and burned into an example. The selection is not random and its pattern is the sermon: in every realm, the judgment fell on those who had received most, position, deliverance, and place, and treated the gift as freedom from the Giver. Jude has not yet described his intruders' conduct in any detail. He has done something colder. He has shown his readers the archive their story will be filed under, and now he turns to the men themselves, in the same way.

title: The Lord Rebuke You
subtitle: Jude 1:8–11
description: Dreamers who slander glorious beings, set against the archangel Michael, who would not slander even the devil but said, The Lord rebuke you; and the woe over Cain's path, Balaam's error, and Korah's rebellion.
paragraphs: The turn onto the intruders themselves takes three charges in one breath: “Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings.” Dreamers is Jude's name for their inner life, men guided by their own visions and appetites rather than the faith once delivered, and the charges run body, order, and speech: they defile their bodies, they reject authority, and they slander glorious beings, beings Jude does not identify beyond his words and the telling does not identify for him. In the same way is the bridge he keeps walking: as the angels fell by leaving their place, these fall by scorning every place above their own, including the unseen ranks they cannot comprehend.

Against the slander he sets one scene, and it is the strangest in the letter: “But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said,” “The Lord rebuke you!” The scene is carried exactly as Jude reports it, and no further: the highest angel, in a dispute with the devil himself, over Moses' body, with every right anger could claim, and he will not pronounce the rebuke as his own. He refers it upward, the Lord rebuke you, and stops his mouth there. If Michael would not slander the devil, Jude's argument runs, what are these men doing slandering glorious beings they do not even understand?

One plain statement about the scene belongs here. The dispute over Moses' body is not narrated anywhere in the Bible's own story of Moses; Jude draws it from tradition outside Scripture, often linked to a lost work called the Assumption of Moses. The telling says that once and builds nothing on the source; what it carries is the point Jude himself makes with it, the archangel's restraint, and lets the origin stand as Jude leaves it, reported and unexplained.

The contrast lands in the next verse like a verdict: “These men, however, slander what they do not understand, and like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively.” Slander upward, at what they do not understand, and instinct downward, knowing their appetites the way animals know theirs, and destroyed by precisely that knowledge. Michael, who understood the unseen world, restrained his tongue; these men, who understand nothing above their instincts, loose theirs on everything. Jude's however is doing heavy work in the sentence: the whole episode hangs on the distance between the archangel's one careful sentence and the dreamers' careless many.

Then the letter pronounces its only woe, and it is a gallery in a single line: “Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed for profit into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion.” Three names, three angles, each carried only as Jude names it and no wider: Cain's path, the brother-hatred that ends in blood, told in Genesis; Balaam's error, prophecy rushed into for profit, told in Numbers; Korah's rebellion, the grasping at a place not given, which swallowed its makers, told in Numbers too. Their full stories stand in their own books in this series, and Jude borrows none of their detail. He needs only the directions: hatred of brothers, greed in holy things, rebellion against God's order. The dreamers, he says, are walking all three roads at once, and every one of the three roads has its end already on record.

title: Hidden Reefs and Wandering Stars
subtitle: Jude 1:12–16
description: The portrait in pictures: hidden reefs at the love feasts, clouds without water, trees twice dead, wild waves foaming shame, wandering stars reserved for blackest darkness; Enoch's prophecy; and the grumblers' sound.
paragraphs: Jude now does something unusual even for him: he stops arguing and simply shows the men, in a run of pictures drawn from the table, the farm, and the sea. The first picture is set at the church's own meal: “These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves.” A reef is the danger a sailor cannot see, and these are hidden at the love feast itself, the congregation's table of fellowship, where they eat without shame and feed, shepherding is his biting word for it, only themselves. The men who crept in unnoticed in verse 4 are unnoticed still, and Jude's pictures are an act of pointing: there, at your own table, under the surface of your own feast.

The pictures turn to weather and harvest: “They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted.” A cloud that promises rain over dry land and delivers nothing is a cruelty in farm country, and Jude makes it worse: these clouds do not even steer themselves, they are carried. A fruitless tree in autumn has missed its one season, and Jude doubles its death, twice dead, dead in fruitlessness and dead in uprooting. Promise without delivery, season without fruit: two pictures of religious men whose whole output is appearance, and the telling lets the pictures stand in his words, unexplained into any system, because the pictures are the explanation.

The last two pictures darken past the farm to the sea and the sky: “They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever.” Wild waves produce only foam, and the foam is their own shame, the one thing their energy manufactures. Wandering stars leave the fixed courses sailors steer by, lights that cannot be navigated from, and their reservation is stated as already made: blackest darkness, forever. Jude's picture-run ends where his judgments began, in darkness kept for a day, and the stars who abandoned their courses join the angels who abandoned their dwelling in the same kept gloom.

Then Jude reaches outside the canon for a voice, and the telling names that plainly once, here: the prophecy he quotes stands in the book called 1 Enoch, which is not part of the Bible, and Genesis itself does not record these words. With that said, the citation is carried as Jude carries it: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them:” and then the words themselves, “Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones” “to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.” Four times ungodly in one sentence, a drumbeat: the coming is not aimed at the world in general but at deeds and harsh words, the exact two currencies the dreamers trade in. What Christians should make of Jude quoting a book outside Scripture has been disagreed about for as long as the letter has been read; the telling states the citation and the disagreement and argues neither side.

The portrait closes with the men's sound: “These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts; their mouths spew arrogance; they flatter others for their own advantage.” Grumbling is the noise of it, discontent as a way of life, mouths full of arrogance, and flattery, the apparent opposite, exposed as the same self-interest wearing its other face: they praise others only for their own advantage. Jude has now shown the intruders in every register he owns, archive, scene, gallery, picture, prophecy, and character sketch. The letter's next word is its great hinge, and it is addressed to the other people in the room: but you, beloved.

title: But You, Beloved, Remember
subtitle: Jude 1:17–19
description: The hinge of the letter: but you, beloved, remember what the apostles foretold, scoffers following their own ungodly desires, the divisive who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit.
paragraphs: The hinge of the letter is two words long: “But you, beloved, remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.” After ten verses of them, Jude turns to his actual audience, and his first word to the beloved is a memory assignment. The crisis is not to be met with panic or with novelty; it is to be recognized. The apostles had described this weather before it arrived, and a church that remembers the forecast reads the storm as confirmation rather than surprise. Remember is the same pastoral instrument Jude used on the judgments in verse 5, fully aware and yet reminded, now pointed at apostolic teaching instead of ancient history.

The saying itself is carried as their words, quoted whole: “when they said to you,” “In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.” Scoffers, in the last times, following their own ungodly desires: the marks are mockery and appetite, scorn aimed at the faith and desire aimed at the self, and both have been on Jude's page since verse 4. The telling builds no timetable on the last-times words and dates nothing by them; they stand as the apostles' foretelling as Jude recalls it, a recognition sign for his readers whenever such men appear, not a clock for any reader's century.

Jude's own verdict on the scoffers is three words deep: “These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit.” Cause divisions is the social fact: these are not lonely heretics but splitters, men whose presence in a congregation produces factions. Worldly is his blunt category, people of the present order only, and devoid of the Spirit is the root he assigns: for all their dream-talk of visions and glorious beings, the one thing they lack is the Spirit of God. The contrast is being loaded for the next sentence, where the beloved will be told to do the very thing these men cannot: pray in the Holy Spirit.

So the remembering episode ends with the church armed at exactly one point, recognition. The intruders are not a surprise attack but a foretold arrival; their scoffing, their appetites, their divisions, and their Spirit-less religion are all on the apostles' record. What remains is the positive charge, and Jude is finished with description now. The letter's last movement will not mention the intruders' deeds again except as the backdrop for mercy, his own included. But you, beloved, is about to become a set of verbs: build, pray, keep, await, and have mercy.

title: Keep Yourselves in the Love of God
subtitle: Jude 1:20–25
description: The charge and the crown: build yourselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God, show mercy in its three grades, and the great doxology to him who is able to keep you.
paragraphs: The charge to the beloved comes as one long sentence, and it begins with construction: “But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit,” Building yourselves up: the church under quiet infiltration is not told to merely endure but to build, and the building material is the same faith once entrusted, now called most holy. Praying in the Holy Spirit stands inside the building work, and it answers the last episode's verdict without comment: the intruders are devoid of the Spirit; the beloved pray in him. The sentence has not reached its main verb yet, and its remaining clause gives the posture that holds the whole letter: keeping, waiting, and mercy.

The sentence completes itself: “keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life.” Keep yourselves is the letter's bookend made into a command. The readers were introduced as kept in Jesus Christ, kept by God; now they are told to keep themselves in his love, God's keeping and their keeping stated side by side without apology or explanation, and this telling carries both as Jude states them. And the waiting is not idle: they await the mercy of the Lord Jesus Christ, mercy again, the letter's first greeting word returning as its last hope, the mercy that will bring eternal life at his coming.

Then the keeping turns outward, in three grades of mercy that Jude distinguishes carefully: “And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt;” Doubters first, the wavering who have not denied anything, met with plain mercy. “save others by snatching them from the fire;” Others stand closer to the flames, and the response escalates from mercy to rescue, snatching language, the shepherd's urgency of the love-feast passage inverted: shepherds who save rather than feed themselves. “and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.” Still others draw mercy in its most careful form, mercy that fears contagion even as it reaches, hating the stained clothing while loving the wearer. The caution is carried alongside the mercy here, exactly as Jude carries it, neither separated nor softened; the rescuer's hatred is for the stain, and the rescue is the point.

And then the servant who began with the least claiming title ends by saying the most claiming words in the letter, and they are not about himself or even about the readers. They are worship: “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy” and then, after the sentence's own break, “to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen.” Able to keep you from stumbling: the whole letter's anxiety, a church that might slip on hidden reefs, is answered by a Keeper who presents his people unblemished and does it with great joy. The doxology reaches in both directions at once, before all time and for all eternity, and the last of the undated letters, the sternest page in the group, closes not on the intruders, not even on the beloved, but on the glory. Amen stands. The series turns next to letters of a different kind, written to a younger worker named Timothy, and they begin with a charge of their own.
